situation:
You are the operations manager at EMBER ROW, a hot sauce and condiment brand that bottles in a leased commercial kitchen. A new president (judge) took over a year ago after two losing years and has cut costs back toward a break-even point the company should reach in about five months. The president (judge) has asked you to recommend how EMBER ROW should run production through the months before then.

Cash is the whole of the problem. A contract with a group of pepper growers commits EMBER ROW to buy their entire harvest, and the peppers all arrive inside six weeks. The leased kitchen can process only part of that volume before the rest spoils, so a share of fruit the company has already paid for would be thrown out.

A co-packer two hours away has offered to bottle everything at the lowest monthly cost EMBER ROW has been quoted, and it could take the whole harvest before any of it spoils. Sending production there means the company hands over its recipe files and its customer list, and the same plant bottles for a direct competitor. If that information gets out, it cannot be taken back.

Keeping production in the leased kitchen protects the recipe files and the customer list, but the kitchen's fixed overhead stays on the books every month, and covering it would mean suspending the printed direct-mail catalog whose copy brings in most of the company's repeat orders. It would also mean telling the growers that EMBER ROW cannot use their whole harvest this year.

The president (judge) wants you to weigh what each course really costs, to say what the company owes the growers and its customers under either one, and to recommend one of them. The president (judge) will greet you and ask to hear your ideas, and after you have presented and answered questions, the president (judge) will thank you for your time.
judgeCharacterization:
You are the president (judge) of EMBER ROW, brought in a year ago after two losing years. Business background is the same as the situation above. You have asked your operations manager to weigh what each course really costs, to say what the company owes the growers and its customers under either one, and to recommend either sending production to the co-packer or keeping it in the leased kitchen.

You will greet the participant and ask to hear their ideas. After the participant has presented, ask the following questions:
judgeQuestions: How would you explain this to the growers?
What would you say if they asked about next year's contract?
